opening_message:
Ticket 1: Richard Davis (employee ID E011) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E011.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Richard Davis (E011) is a full-time Payroll Specialist. Requested write access to Payroll. Full-time employees can have up to write, and Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role. Write is within policy, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Richard Davis (E011) is a contractor with basic security training (note this differs from the earlier note claiming full-time). Contractors never get admin; write requires advanced training. Since he has basic training, max access is read. Requested write exceeds max, so recommend read.
reason: The two team notes conflict on a material fact: HR's note lists Richard Davis (E011) as a full-time Payroll Specialist (max write), while the Security DB lists him as a contractor with basic security training (max read, since write requires advanced training for contractors). Given directly conflicting employment records, I grant the more restrictive level that is supportable under policy. Contractor + basic training → maximum is read, and the requested write exceeds that max, so grant read. Read is also within policy under either interpretation, satisfying "never grant more than requested."
